title: Repent a day before you die (Avot 2:10)
hookLine: Rabbi Eliezer: repent one day before your death, and no one knows the day, so every day
last: EVERYTHING ELSE GROWS FROM THE HEART.

cards: Rabbi Eliezer's students heard him say something that sounded impossible: repent one day before your death. So they asked the obvious question. How is anyone supposed to know which day that is?
Eliezer was one of yesterday's five, the one his own teacher compared to a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. He had heard a great deal and lost none of it.
And his answer takes a far-off day and sets it down right here, in this one.

teach.b: He said three things. Let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own. Don't be quick to anger.
And repent one day before your death. That last one is the riddle, and the Talmud records his answer to the students.
Does anyone know the day he'll die? All the more reason to repent today, in case you die tomorrow. Then all your days will be spent in repentance.
The word is teshuvah. It's usually translated repentance, but it really means return, or turning. You notice you've wandered off the path, and you turn back toward it.
No groveling, no drama. Just a turn. Then a parable.

A king invited his servants to a banquet, but didn't say when. The wise ones dressed in their best and waited by the palace door: a palace is never short of anything, so the feast could start any minute.
The foolish ones went off to their work, saying there's no banquet without a lot of preparation first. Suddenly the king called them in. The wise walked in dressed and ready.
The foolish came in dirty from work, and weren't allowed to sit at the table.

teach.h: LET THY GARMENTS BE ALWAYS WHITE.
teach.b: The verse that goes with it is in Ecclesiastes, which in the JPS translation reads, "Let thy garments be always white." Not out of fear. Just ready.
Eliezer's advice isn't a threat. It's a schedule. If today might be the day, then today is the day to turn.

how: Jewish tradition treats teshuvah, returning, as possible every day, not only on Yom Kippur, and the traditional bedtime prayers include a moment of forgiving others before sleep.

o: a punishment paid to make up for a sin
returning: turning back toward the right path
a fast for forgiveness on Yom Kippur

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: dressed and waiting at the door

s: Rabbi Eliezer claimed to know the day of his death
his point was that nobody knows, so repent today.
teshuvah literally means turning or returning
you notice you've wandered, and you turn back.
in the parable, the foolish servants were ready when the king called
they came in dirty from work. the wise were dressed and waiting.

games.q: you're a servant. the king has invited you to a banquet but hasn't said when. what do you do?
o: go to work. there'll be plenty of warning.
dress in your best and wait by the door.
ask the other servants to cover for you.
games.why: the wise servants waited, dressed and ready, and walked straight in. let thy garments be always white.

practice: Look back over the day so far, slowly, from waking up until now, and notice one moment where you drifted from the person you mean to be: a sharp word, a shortcut, a kindness skipped.
Don't argue with it or punish yourself; just name it, and picture one small step back in the right direction. If you pray, you can bring it to God.

wordCard.voice: Teshuvah. Return, a turning back: Rabbi Eliezer's riddle solved by turning today, since nobody knows the day of death.

orig.note: Hebrew: repentance, literally a turning back.

carryVoice: Your line: repent today. Teshuvah is a turn, not a trial. Day two fifty-eight, done.
